pipeline_name: Russian Federation – Turkey Natural Gas Main Transmission Line

validity.researcher_notes: The Russia to Turkey line is real. The 2015 BOTAS report and a Turkish regulator source quoted in a thesis give 845 and 842 km. Russian gas stopped using the Trans-Balkan route on 1 January 2020 and now arrives by TurkStream, but the Turkish section stays in use.

fills.researcher_notes: The 2015 annual report of BOTAS, the Turkish state gas company, lists a western supply contract with the Russian Federation of 4 billion cubic meters a year. That is the volume contracted for this line, not a stated design capacity of the pipe, so the tier is medium. The sheet value of 4 bcm/y stands.

verifications.note: 24-36 in; thesis Table 10: 36 and 24 inch sections
24-36 in; thesis Table 10: 36 and 24 inch sections

fills.researcher_notes: The BOTAS 2015 annual report gives a diameter of 24 to 36 inches for the line. A 2012 Iowa State thesis table of the Malkoclar to Ankara line lists 36 inch pipe from Malkoclar to Ambarli and Pendik and 24 inch pipe on the later sections. Both agree with the sheet value of 24 and 36 inches.

The BOTAS 2015 annual report gives a length of 845 km for the Russian Federation to Turkey line. The Iowa State thesis says 842 km, quoting a 2011 Turkish regulator source, so the two differ by 3 km. The sheet value of 845 km matches the BOTAS report exactly. The thesis is not counted as a second source because it disagrees slightly.

verifications.note: Ankara reached August 1988; gas supplied October 1988
Ankara reached August 1988; gas supplied October 1988

fills.researcher_notes: The BOTAS 2015 annual report says the Thrace part started operating in 1987 and the rest in 1988, and its project table gives a completion date of July 1989. The Iowa State thesis says the line reached the Bulgarian border crossing at Malkoclar in 1986, Hamitabat in June 1987 and Ankara in August 1988, with gas supplied to Ankara in October 1988. The whole line was therefore running in 1988. The sheet year of 1988 stands. The 1987 date is only the first section.

The BOTAS 2015 annual report lists the line among the pipelines of the Turkish state gas company, which owns and runs the national transmission system. The report does not use the word owner for this line in particular, so the tier is medium. The sheet spells it BOTAŞ and the ownership team style is BOTAŞ AŞ; the owner is otherwise unchanged.

The blank Operator cell was not filled. The BOTAS annual report describes the company as running the transmission system but no cited page names an operator for this line in so many words. Not searched beyond the wiki citations this pass.

fills.researcher_notes: The BOTAS 2015 annual report lists the line as in operation. The Neftegaz article says Gazprom stopped supplying Turkey through the Trans-Balkan route on 1 January 2020 and moved the flow to TurkStream, while the Turkish section was used in April 2023 for a test delivery in reverse, from Turkey to Bulgaria. The Turkish section is therefore still in service as part of the BOTAS network. Operating stands.

status_reviews.researcher_notes: BOTAS lists the line as in operation. Russian deliveries through the Bulgarian crossing ended on 1 January 2020 but the Turkish section carried a reverse test flow in April 2023, so it is still in use.

summary: Russia-Turkey line: all values confirmed by BOTAS 2015 report, owner restyled to BOTAŞ AŞ, operator not found
